title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 52
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Animals Behind Glass
passages.text:
A. Collections of captive animals are ancient and were, for most of their history, displays of the power of whoever owned them. Exotic creatures arrived as tribute or as trophies, were kept in conditions that killed them quickly, and were replaced from the same sources; the purpose was to demonstrate reach rather than to sustain a population, and nothing about the arrangement required the animals to thrive.

B. The public institution that replaced the private collection changed the audience without initially changing much else. Admission was opened, the stated purpose became education, and the enclosures remained small, hard-surfaced and designed for visibility — the animal placed where it could always be seen, which is the opposite of what most species do when they can choose. The building served the visitor and the collection served the building.

C. Reform came from the animals' behaviour rather than from argument. Repetitive movements — pacing a fixed route, swaying, over-grooming — were observed to increase in barren enclosures and to decrease when the animal was given complexity, choice and something to do, and this provided a measurable signal that was harder to dismiss than an appeal to sentiment. Enclosure design changed once there was a number attached to the problem.

D. The modern justification rests on four claims of unequal strength. Conservation breeding has demonstrably returned several species to the wild, and is relevant to a small number of species; research on captive animals produces knowledge unobtainable otherwise, and much of it concerns captivity itself; education is asserted more often than it is measured; and funding for field conservation is real and modest relative to the cost of the institution generating it.

E. The measurement problem in the education claim is genuine rather than evasive. Visitors leave able to name animals they have seen, and the evidence that a visit changes behaviour towards conservation afterwards is weak, partly because such changes are hard to detect and partly because the visit is a short event in a long life. Institutions have responded by studying it more honestly than the criticism usually assumes.

F. The species question is what the argument now turns on. A large mammal that ranges over great distances and lives in complex groups cannot be given anything resembling its natural circumstances in any enclosure that can be built, while many smaller animals can be kept in conditions that meet their requirements fully. The defensible position is not a judgement about zoos in general but a different answer for different species, which is harder to argue and easier to act on.

passages.title: Cities Without Planners
passages.text:
A termite mound is built by insects that cannot see the structure they are producing, have no representation of it, and act only on what is immediately in front of them. The mound nonetheless has a stable internal climate, a system of passages that circulates air, and a shape adapted to the local sun and wind. Explaining how the second follows from the first is the central question in the study of insect societies, and the answer changed what people thought organisation required.

The mechanism is that the structure itself carries the instructions. An insect deposits material where a stimulus is present; the deposit changes the stimulus; the changed stimulus prompts the next action, from that insect or another. No individual holds a plan, no individual issues instructions, and the sequence is stored in the shape of the work rather than in any head. The building tells the builders what to do next.

Division of labour arises the same way and is less fixed than it appears. Individuals in many species take on tasks according to age, size or how much of a particular stimulus they encounter, and a colony deprived of a class of workers reallocates others to that work without anything resembling a decision. The apparent organisation chart is an outcome of local rules and thresholds rather than an assignment.

The queen is the most persistent misunderstanding and the term is the problem. She does not direct anything: she lays eggs, and her chemical signals convey information about her presence and condition to which others respond, which is a very different thing from command. Colonies do not have a decision-maker, and their most impressive collective behaviour — selecting a new nest site, allocating foragers between food sources — is produced by competing signals resolving into a choice without anyone making it.

The comparison with human organisations is where the field is most often overinterpreted. Insect colonies achieve robustness, redundancy and adaptation with no manager, which is genuinely instructive; they also achieve it with genetically near-identical members whose interests barely conflict, over evolutionary time, with no requirement that any individual be persuaded. Lifting the mechanism into a setting where those conditions do not hold has produced more metaphor than method.

What the study has changed most is the assumption that complexity implies a designer. The mound, the foraging network and the colony's response to disturbance all look like the products of a plan and are produced by simple rules operating repeatedly in a structure that records what has already been done. That is a general finding about how order arises, and it applies well beyond insects.

passages.title: Taxing the Ground
passages.text:
Land has a property that almost nothing else has: its quantity does not respond to price. A tax on buildings discourages building, a tax on income discourages earning, and a tax on transactions discourages transacting, but a tax on the value of land cannot reduce the amount of land, because that amount is fixed regardless of what is charged for it. This is the argument for land value taxation, it has been understood for centuries, and it has been adopted almost nowhere in full.

The reasoning about who ends up paying is the part most often got wrong. Ordinary taxes are partly passed on — a tax on a business appears in its prices, a tax on rented property is shared between owner and tenant according to how each responds — but a landowner charging the highest rent the market will bear cannot raise it because a tax has been imposed, since the tenant's willingness to pay is unchanged. The burden stays with the owner, which is the source of both the theoretical appeal and the political difficulty.

What makes the value in the first place is the argument's foundation. A plot is valuable because of what surrounds it: the transport, the schools, the businesses, the other people, and the public investment that produced most of them. The owner did not create that value, and taxing it recovers for the public a return on what the public built — an argument that persuades people who agree on very little else.

The practical objections are real and mostly soluble. Valuing land separately from what stands on it is a genuine technical task and is performed routinely by assessors in several jurisdictions; asset-rich, income-poor owners face a real cash problem, which is addressed by deferring liability against the eventual sale; and transition is disruptive because existing owners bought at prices that assumed no such tax. The last is the serious one and it is a transition problem rather than an objection to the design.

The effect on land use is what most attracts its supporters. A charge on value regardless of what is built there penalises holding a valuable central site empty or underused, which is currently costless to the owner and expensive to everyone else, and encourages development where infrastructure already exists. Where partial versions have been implemented, the observed effect on development in central areas is positive and modest rather than transformative.

The honest summary is that the theory is stronger than the evidence, because the evidence is thin. Full implementations are rare, partial ones are confounded by everything else happening in those places, and the enormous claims made by the most enthusiastic advocates rest on the argument rather than on measurement. It remains among the least distorting ways to raise revenue and is not the single reform its supporters have often described.
